titre: The Seveso Leak Invents the European Directive
accroche: On July 10, 1976, a valve gives way near Milan and releases a cloud of dioxin. Six years later, Europe regulates this industrial risk for the first time.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 10, 1976, at about 12:37 p.m., a safety valve gives way on a reactor at the chemical plant Industrie Chimiche Meda Società Azionaria (ICMESA) in Meda, about twelve miles north of Milan. A white cloud escapes and falls on the neighboring town of Seveso and the surrounding municipalities. It contains 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD), one of the most toxic compounds known to chemists, released in an estimated quantity of between 15 and 30 kilograms. ICMESA is a subsidiary of the Swiss group Givaudan, itself a subsidiary of the pharmaceutical group Hoffmann-La Roche.

## A Gap Discovered After the Fact

No one is killed on the spot, but the scale of the cloud is understood only slowly. The evacuation of the most contaminated area, known as Zone A, begins only fifteen days after the accident and is completed only on August 2, 1976, with the removal of about 730 residents. Six hundred forty people in the region develop chloracne, a skin condition caused by massive exposure to dioxin. The investigation that follows reveals a structural defect rather than simple negligence: no common rule required the plant to tell the local authorities the exact nature of the products it handled, or to give them any emergency plan in case of a leak.

## A Directive That Never Names Seveso

On June 24, 1982, the Council of the European Communities adopts Directive 82/501/EEC on the major-accident hazards of certain industrial activities, published in the Official Journal on August 5, 1982. The text requires operators of hazardous installations to notify the authorities of the nature of their activities and to prepare internal and external emergency plans; Member States must transpose these obligations before January 8, 1984, and extend them to already existing installations before January 8, 1985. The text itself never names Seveso: its preamble merely notes that “such accidents have already occurred in the Community.” It is usage, not the law, that christened this text the “Seveso Directive,” and it will take its third version, in 2012, for the name finally to enter a European text, alongside Bhopal, Toulouse, and three other industrial disasters cited as the reason for the system's existence. The shift lies in the order of things: it is not a law that produced vigilance, it is the lack of vigilance that produced the law: six years after the events, and never quite in time for the next accident.

repere.texte: European Directive 82/501/EEC of June 24, 1982, adopted after the Seveso accident, requires Member States to transpose its notification and emergency-plan obligations before January 8, 1984, and to extend them to already existing installations before January 8, 1985.
repere.source: Council Directive 82/501/EEC of 24 June 1982 on the major-accident hazards of certain industrial activities, Official Journal of the European Communities L 230 of August 5, 1982

carte.punch: A dioxin leak near Milan invents the first European law on industrial risk.
carte.idee: On July 10, 1976, a valve gives way at the ICMESA plant near Milan and spreads a cloud of dioxin over an entire valley. Six years later, in 1982, the European Community requires hazardous plants for the first time to declare their risks and prepare an emergency plan.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Directive 2012/18/EU (“Seveso III”), which cites Seveso by name
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The third revision of the text, in force since 2015, after two interim updates in 1996 and 2003.

quiz.question: Why did the 1976 Seveso accident reveal a legal gap rather than a simple operating error?
choix: Because Italian law at the time explicitly allowed the release of dioxin into the atmosphere
Because no common rule required the plant to declare its hazardous activities or to plan for emergencies
Because the European Community had no competence at the time to legislate on the chemical industry
Because the ICMESA plant escaped all tax oversight by the Italian state
quiz.explication: The investigation showed that no common rule required the notification of risks or an emergency plan: it is this gap, not an isolated act of negligence, that the 1982 directive corrects.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which extremely toxic chemical escaped from the ICMESA plant on July 10, 1976?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The cloud contained 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD), released in an estimated quantity of between 15 and 30 kilograms, one of the most toxic compounds known.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long after the accident did the evacuation of the most contaminated area begin?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The evacuation of Zone A began only fifteen days after the accident and was completed only on August 2, 1976, with the removal of about 730 residents.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the preamble of the 2012 “Seveso III” directive say that the 1982 text did not?
choix: It names Seveso explicitly, alongside Bhopal and Toulouse, as the justification for the system
It transfers all competence over industrial risk to the United Nations
It removes the notification requirement for small installations
It sets, for the first time, a capped fine applicable in all Member States
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Unlike the 1982 text, which never named Seveso, the preamble of the 2012 directive explicitly cites “the accidents of Seveso, Bhopal, Schweizerhalle, Enschede, Toulouse and Buncefield.”
